links.note: 651 says the goodness of support (துணைநலம்) gives ஆக்கம், while the goodness of action (வினைநலம்) gives 'வேண்டிய எல்லாம்'. 457 uses the same frame, மனநலம் giving ஆக்கம் and இனநலம் giving 'எல்லாப் புகழும்'. In both, one good yields prosperity and a second yields everything, but the lesser term in 651 (companions) is close to the greater term in 457 (company), so the two rankings are worth reading together.

651 sets வினைநலம் above துணைநலம்: support gives only ஆக்கம், good action gives all that is wanted. 455 says purity of mind and purity of action (செய்வினை தூய்மை) both come leaning on purity of company (இனந்தூய்மை தூவா வரும்). Read together, the action that 651 ranks above one's support is itself said to depend on the people one keeps.

652 says one must always shun 'புகழொடு நன்றி பயவா வினை', action that yields neither renown nor good. 439, among the faults a ruler must guard against, says 'நயவற்க நன்றி பயவா வினை': do not set your heart on action that yields no good. The same phrase appears as a minister's rule of action and as a ruler's rule of desire, with 652 adding புகழ் and 'என்றும்'.

653 tells those who say 'ஆஅதும்' (we shall rise) to stop doing what dims their ஒளி. 962 says those who want சீர் together with பேராண்மை will not do 'சீரல்ல' even for the sake of சீர். 962 takes the harder case 653 leaves open: the dimming deed may itself be a route to fame, and it is still refused.

653 treats ஒளி as something the ambitious ('ஆஅதும் என்னுமவர்') must protect by refraining from certain deeds. 971 defines ஒளி as 'உள்ள வெறுக்கை', abundance of spirit, and இளி as saying one will live without it. Together they give ஒளி two sides: it is lost by what one does (653) and it consists in what one aspires to (971).

654: those of 'நடுக்கற்ற காட்சி' will not do degrading things (இளிவந்த செய்யார்) even when in trouble. 699: those of 'துளக்கற்ற காட்சி' will not do unacceptable things (கொள்ளாத செய்யார்) on the thought that they are in the king's favour. The same figure of unshaken sight, with the same 'செய்யார்', is tested once by distress and once by favour, so steadiness is shown under both pressure and licence.

654 says those of unshaken sight do nothing degrading even in distress (இடுக்கண் படினும்). 174 says those of 'புன்மையில் காட்சி' who have conquered the senses will not covet on the plea 'இலம்' (we have nothing). Both verses name a clear-sighted person (காட்சியவர்) and deny that need is an excuse; 174 applies it to coveting, 654 to action generally.

654: clear-sighted people do not do what is degrading even when trouble comes. 218: those of 'கடனறி காட்சி' do not falter in ஒப்புரவு even in a season without means (இடனில் பருவத்தும் ... ஒல்கார்). One verse says hardship does not make them do wrong, the other that it does not make them stop doing good; the two are the negative and positive halves of the same steadiness.

655 says not to do things one will lament with 'எற்று' (what have I done), using இரங்குவ. 535 describes the person who slipped by not guarding beforehand and afterwards 'இரங்கி விடும்' over his own error. 535 shows the regret 655 warns of and locates its cause in the failure to guard in advance. The second half of 655 is read differently by the commentators (Parimelazhagar: do not go on lamenting; Kalaignar: do not repeat the deed), and this link rests only on the first half.

655 asks that one not do what will be regretted afterwards. 467 says to think and then resolve (எண்ணித் துணிக), and calls it a lapse to say 'we will think after resolving'. Both put the reflection before the act: 467 as a rule of planning, 655 as a rule about the purity of the deed.

656: even if one sees one's own mother hungry (ஈன்றாள் பசி காண்பான் ஆயினும்), do not do what the worthy condemn. 327: even if one's own life must go (தன்னுயிர் நீப்பினும்), do not do the deed that takes another's life. Both use 'செய்யற்க' with an extreme concession, one in the chapter on not killing and one in the chapter on a minister's clean action, showing the book's habit of stating a prohibition at its hardest case.

656 forbids the blameworthy deed even when the need is a mother's hunger. 961 says to give up things that would diminish one (குன்ற வருப விடல்) even if they are indispensable (இன்றி அமையாச் சிறப்பின ஆயினும்). Both deny that necessity licenses a degrading act; 961 states the principle abstractly under honour, 656 gives it a concrete and painful instance.

656 uses the mother who bore one (ஈன்றாள்) as the strongest pull toward wrongdoing for the sake of relief. 1047 says that one in poverty not joined with virtue (அறஞ்சாரா நல்குரவு) is looked on as a stranger even by the mother who bore him (ஈன்ற தாயானும்). The mother marks the limit case in both: 656 holds conduct firm against her need, while 1047 says poverty without virtue loses even her regard.

657: the extreme poverty of the worthy (சான்றோர் கழிநல்குரவு) is better than wealth got by taking on blame (பழிமலைந்து எய்திய ஆக்கம்). 408: wealth lodged with the unlearned (கல்லார்கண் பட்ட திரு) is more painful than poverty lodged with the good (நல்லார்கண் பட்ட வறுமை). The same comparison of good people's poverty with bad people's wealth is made from each side, once about how wealth was got and once about who holds it.

657 ranks the utter poverty of the worthy above blame-laden wealth. 988 says poverty (இன்மை) is no disgrace (இளிவன்று) to one who has the firmness called சால்பு. 988 supplies the ground for 657's ranking: for the சான்றோர் poverty carries no இளிவு, whereas the wealth in 657 carries பழி.

658: forbidden deeds done without shunning them bring anguish even if they succeed (முடிந்தாலும் பீழை தரும்). 113: give up at once gain that comes from leaving fairness, even if it brings nothing but good (நன்றே தரினும்). Both concede success in advance and still reject the act, so the objection is not that such means fail.

658 says forbidden actions bring anguish even when they are accomplished. 931 says not to want gambling even if one wins (வென்றிடினும்), since the winnings are like the hook a fish has swallowed. The gambling verse gives an image for 658's claim: the success itself is what carries the harm.

658 warns that the gain of a forbidden deed turns to பீழை later. 177 says not to want gain that comes by coveting (வெஃகியாம் ஆக்கம்), because at the time of enjoying it the fruit is hard to make good (விளைவயின் மாண்டற்கு அரிதாம் பயன்). Both place the harm at the stage of the result and not at the stage of getting.

659: everything taken by making others weep leaves with weeping (அழக் கொண்ட எல்லாம் அழப்போம்). 555: the tears of those who weep under oppression they cannot bear (அழுத கண்ணீர்) are the weapon that wears away wealth (செல்வத்தைத் தேய்க்கும் படை). 555 applies the same idea to a king and names the tears themselves as the agent of the loss that 659 only states.

659 says what is taken with tears goes with tears. 283 says gain made by stealth (களவினால் ஆகிய ஆக்கம்) perishes beyond measure even while it seems to grow (ஆவது போலக் கெடும்). Both hold that wrongly got wealth does not stay; 283 adds that it looks like growth first.

The second half of 659 says what comes from good ways (நற்பாலவை) yields later even if it is lost (இழப்பினும் பிற்பயக்கும்). 112 says the wealth of a person of rectitude (செப்பம் உடையவன் ஆக்கம்) does not decay and is a security for those who come after (எச்சத்திற்கு ஏமாப்பு). Both give rightly got wealth a benefit that outlasts the moment, 659 for the person later and 112 for descendants.

660 compares making wealth by deceit (சலத்தால் பொருள்செய்து) and securing oneself with it to pouring water into a pot of unfired clay (பசுமண் கலத்துள் நீர்). 755 says accumulation of wealth that does not come with அருள் and அன்பு should be let go. Parimelazhagar, commenting on 755, explains the reason with this same image of water in an unfired pot, so he reads the two verses as one teaching: 660 gives the image and 755 the rule for a king's revenue.

660: wealth made by deceit is water kept in an unfired clay vessel. 1000: great wealth obtained by one without character is good milk spoiled by the fault of its vessel (கலந்தீமையால் திரிந்தற்று). Both use a faulty கலம் for wealth that cannot be kept, but the fault differs: in 660 it is how the wealth was made, in 1000 it is the holder's character.

661: firmness in action is a person's firmness of mind (மனத்திட்பம்); everything else is something other (மற்றைய எல்லாம் பிற). 34: being spotless in mind (மனத்துக்கண் மாசிலன் ஆதல்) is all of virtue; the rest is noisy show (ஆகுல நீர பிற). The two verses have the same shape, reducing a whole domain to a state of mind and dismissing the remainder as 'பிற', once for virtue and once for effective action.

661 locates firmness in action in the mind and sets other things aside. 600 says a person's real strength (உரம்) is abundance of spirit (உள்ள வெறுக்கை), and those without it are trees. Both place strength within the person; Parimelazhagar's note on 661 lists the outer things meant by 'மற்றைய' as the firmness of army, fort and allies.

662 gives two rules as the way of those who have studied the matter: avoid harm (ஊறொரால்) and do not give way once it has come (உற்றபின் ஒல்காமை). 442 tells a king to cherish those who remove the trouble that has come (உற்றநோய் நீக்கி) and guard beforehand against what has not (உறாஅமை முற்காக்கும்). The same before-and-after pair appears as the doer's own discipline in 662 and as the quality to look for in advisers in 442.

429 says those whose understanding guards against what is coming (எதிரதாக் காக்கும் அறிவினார்) have no affliction that comes to shake them. 662 keeps that first rule (ஊறொரால்) but adds a second for when harm arrives anyway (உற்றபின் ஒல்காமை). 662 thus allows that foresight is not always enough; Parimelazhagar reads the second case as a task spoiled by fate.

663: the right way to act is so that the deed becomes known only at its end (கடைக்கொட்க); if it becomes known midway (இடைக்கொட்கின்) it brings trouble that cannot be undone. 590: do not honour a spy where others can know it (சிறப்பறிய ... செய்யற்க); if the king does, he has himself let out the secret (புறப்படுத்தான் ஆகும் மறை). Both treat premature disclosure as a self-inflicted failure, in a minister's undertaking and in a king's use of spies.

664: saying is easy for anyone; doing as one has said (சொல்லிய வண்ணம் செயல்) is hard. 819: the bond with those whose deed is one thing and word another (வினைவேறு சொல்வேறு பட்டார்) is bitter even in a dream. 664 states the gap between word and deed as a difficulty of execution; 819 judges the same gap in a friend as a fault of character.

664 contrasts easy speech with the difficulty of doing what was said. 640 says those without practical capacity (திறப்பாடு இலாதவர்) leave things unfinished even after planning them in proper order (முறைப்படச் சூழ்ந்தும் முடிவிலவே செய்வர்). Both mark the distance between an account of the deed and the deed; Parimelazhagar reads 'சொல்லுதல்' in 664 as stating in order how a task will be done, which brings it close to 640's planning.

no_link_reason: The meaning of 'ஊறெய்தி' is uncertain (Parimelazhagar takes it as reaching the king; Kalaignar as winning the ruler's regard), and any link would rest on one reading of that phrase.

links.note: 666: those who have planned obtain what they planned as they planned it (எண்ணிய எண்ணியாங்கு எய்துப), if they are firm (திண்ணியர்). 540: it is easy to obtain what one has thought of (உள்ளியது எய்தல் எளிது), if one can keep thinking of what one thought of (உள்ளியது உள்ளப் பெறின்). Both make attainment conditional with 'பெறின்' on a quality of mind, firmness in one and unforgetting attention in the other.

666 uses the formula 'எண்ணிய எண்ணியாங்கு எய்துப' for what the firm obtain. 265 uses the matching formula 'வேண்டிய வேண்டியாங்கு எய்தலால்' for what தவம் obtains, as the reason austerity is practised here. The repeated wording gives firmness in worldly action the same promise that the first book gives austerity; Parimelazhagar places 265's fruits in the next life.

666: what one has thought of is obtained as thought, if one is firm. 309: all one has thought of is obtained at once (உள்ளிய தெல்லாம் உடனெய்தும்), if one does not think of anger in the heart. The same promise is attached to two different inner conditions, one positive (firmness) and one negative (absence of anger).

667: do not scorn anyone on seeing their form (உருவுகண்டு எள்ளாமை), for there are people like the linchpin (அச்சாணி) of a great rolling chariot. 1032: those who plough are the ஆணி of the world's people, because they bear all who cannot plough and take up other work. Both use the pin that holds the wheel for someone small in appearance on whom everything turns; 667 leaves the person unnamed and 1032 names the farmer. Parimelazhagar supplies the smallness in 667 from the simile.

667 says not to judge by form (உரு), because the small-looking may be the linchpin. 279 says the arrow is straight but cruel and the lute bent but good, so people are to be taken by the nature of their deeds (வினைபடு பாலால் கொளல்). Both refuse appearance as the measure and point to function, 279 in the context of false ascetics and 667 in the context of capable agents.

668: in a task one has seen clearly and decided on (கலங்காது கண்ட வினை), act without wavering and without delay (தூக்கங் கடிந்து). 671, opening the next chapter, says deliberation ends in reaching resolve (துணிவு) and it is bad for that resolve to rest in delay (தாழ்ச்சியுள் தங்குதல் தீது). The same rule closes the chapter on firmness and opens the chapter on method: once the thinking is done, delay is the fault.

467 says to think and then resolve on a task, and that saying 'we will think after resolving' is a lapse. 668 takes up from that point: once the task has been seen without confusion (கலங்காது கண்ட), act without wavering (துளங்காது). Together they give a sequence in which doubt belongs before the decision and not after it.

669: do with resolve the deed that yields joy (இன்பம் பயக்கும் வினை), even though pain comes close at first (துன்பம் உறவரினும்). 615: one who does not want pleasure but wants the work (இன்பம் விழையான் வினை விழைவான்) is a pillar who wipes away his kin's துன்பம். Both set இன்பம், துன்பம் and வினை against each other; 669 justifies bearing pain by the joy the deed yields, while 615 describes a doer who is not after pleasure at all and whose work removes others' pain.

669 says to carry through the worthwhile deed despite the pain it brings at first. 611 says one must not slacken on the thought that a thing is hard (அருமை உடைத்தென்று அசாவாமை), since effort gives the greatness needed. Both refuse the difficulty of a task as a reason to hold back; 611 speaks of effort and 669 of resolve (துணிவு).

670: whatever other firmness they have attained (எனைத்திட்பம் எய்தியக் கண்ணும்), the world does not want those who do not want firmness in action. 750: whatever excellences it has (எனைமாட்சித்து ஆகியக் கண்ணும்), a fort is nothing with those who lack excellence in action (வினைமாட்சி இல்லார்கண்). The two chapter-closing verses are built alike and make the same point, that other strengths count for nothing without the capacity to act, once of a minister and once of a fort's defenders.
